This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI.

On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic.

Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public.

There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. 

But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. 

In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work.

Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution.

Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective:

* Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure.

* Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis.

* Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region.

* Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete.

* Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline.

Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.

Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future. The ability to throw compute at problems that you can massively parallelize will be too useful to not take advantage of. 

Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this as it’s a space where testing vast number of permutations of attacks (without getting tired or bored) is an incredibly useful property. You have a wide search space of possible risk vectors and you generally need to be able to chain together different scenarios to achieve the exploit. 

This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times. Super interesting times in cyber.

Gemini 4 Argon is now GA. Argon ranks equal to GPT-6 Astra on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 60% of the Cost per Task with discounted prices until Nov 30

Key takeaways:
- Google is back to having a frontier model released to the public: This is Google's first proprietary model above the Flash class in over 7 months

- Pricing temporarily discounted to 50% until November 30: Gemini 4 Argon has a Cost per Task of $1.99 with discounted prices, a ~40% reduction compared to GPT-6 Astra (max) for a comparable level of Intelligence. It is currently priced at $2/$10 per 1M input/output tokens with a 95% discount for cache reads (up from 90% from previous Gemini models). Prices will increase to $4/$20 after November 30

- Large improvements in agentic performance: Gemini 4 Argon shows substantial improvements in agentic evaluations such as AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal Bench 4. This is an area in which Google's models have historically underperformed compared to leading peers

Lowest hallucination rate among leading models: On AA-Omniscience, Gemini 4 Argon has a 15% hallucination rate, the lowest of any model scoring 45+ on the Intelligence Index

Introducing the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, benchmarking decision models across classification, tool calling, knowledge and reasoning. Jev leads among decision models; language models such as Claude Haiku 5.5 still deliver higher accuracy, but at much higher cost and latency

Decision models deliver structured answers or classifications with associated probabilities, offering faster responses and lower costs than using language models. The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0 compares the capability, cost, and speed of decision models and also compares to language models.

Benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v1.0:

➤ AA-Omniscience-Decision: A private dataset of 500 questions adapted from the proprietary AA-Omniscience benchmark, measuring decision models’ knowledge and tendency to hallucinate

➤ HLE-MultiChoice: 513 text-only multiple-choice questions from Humanity’s Last Exam, testing decision models’ reasoning capabilities

➤ When2Call: A tool-calling benchmark from NVIDIA, testing whether models can correctly decide to call a tool, request clarification, decline to answer, or respond directly, evaluating capabilities relevant to agentic workflows and tool routing

➤ WildGuardTest: A safety benchmark evaluating models’ classification capabilities across harmful user requests, assistant refusals, and harmful responses. We use a subset of 835 of the original 1,725 test rows where all three human annotators agreed on all three labels, after excluding questions that consistently trigger model refusals

Key results:

➤ Jev 1.13 leads the Decision Index, and sits on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier: Jev 1.13 from @typesafeai scores 58 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index, ahead of GLiDE (54) from @fastinoAI and Microsoft-Decision-1 (54) from @Microsoft. Decider v1.1 27B from @perplexity_ai has the lowest Cost per 1M Tasks at $17, with Microsoft-Decision-1 ($31) and Jev 1.13 ($42) also on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. Celeris-1 Decision has the fastest Time per Task at 0.06 seconds, more than 2x faster than Jev 1.13 (0.13 seconds per task)

➤ Decision models are poorly calibrated on knowledge and reasoning tasks: Across almost all probability levels for chosen answers, accuracy falls below that probability for all decision models. This gap is largest on AA-Omniscience-Decision and HLE-MultiChoice, while most models are relatively well-calibrated on WildGuardTest (classification) and When2Call (tool calling)

➤ Decision models offer significant speed and cost advantages over language models, but trail on knowledge and reasoning: On classification and tool-calling tasks, leading decision models perform comparably to language models while being significantly faster and cheaper. However, language models substantially outperform on knowledge and reasoning. Claude Haiku 5.5 (Low) scores 61 on the Decision Index, 3 points ahead of Jev 1.13, but takes 1.4 seconds per task vs. 0.13 seconds (11x slower) and costs $184 per 1M Tasks vs. $42 for Jev 1.13 (4.4x more expensive)

We will continue to develop the Artificial Analysis Decision Index to help developers and companies better understand when and how to use decision models.

Cache hit rates and Cost per Task by provider are now live on Artificial Analysis: Cost per Task for GLM-5.3 (max) varies ~9x across providers, driven by a combination of cache hit rate and token pricing

Agentic workloads resend the full conversation history every turn, so most input tokens are cacheable, and cache pricing and cache hit rates drive most of the gap in Cost per Task. We already use measured cache hit rates to calculate Cost per Task, and are now publishing them for each model endpoint we track.

What's new:
➤ Cache hit rates are now visible for all first-party and third-party endpoints, measured by running multi-turn agentic coding tasks and reading cached tokens from each provider's usage response. Cache hit rate is the share of cacheable input tokens served from cache.
➤ Cost per Task is now available by provider for open weights models, calculated from each provider's input, output, cache hit and cache write prices, applied at its measured cache hit rate. To standardize across providers for a given model, we use the same input, output and cacheable token counts from the model's Intelligence Index run.

Key takeaways:
➤ Cost per Task on GLM-5.3 (max) spans ~9x across providers, from $0.92 on Makora to $8.68 on Nebius. Both serve nearly all cacheable input from cache (98% and 100%) and charge the same output price ($4.40 per 1M tokens), so the gap comes from input pricing: Makora charges $0.10 per 1M cached input tokens, while Nebius offers no cached input discount on its shared serverless endpoints and bills all input at the full $1.40.
➤ Cache hit rate ranges from 41% to 100% across 21 providers (25 endpoints). 15 endpoints are at 98% or above, and eight are at 100%: Modal, DeepInfra, Parasail, Together AI, DigitalOcean, Nebius, Novita and Z AI's first-party API. Multiverse Computing is lowest at 41%, followed by Bitdeer at 50%.

Fish Audio's Drama 3 Preview is the new #1 open-weights Text to Speech model on the Artificial Analysis Text to Speech leaderboard. The model also leads all models in our Pronunciation Robustness leaderboard, ahead of Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo

Drama 3 Preview is the new open weights Text to Speech model from @FishAudio, built for multi-character scenes and long-form content with voice cloning and natural-language control. Weights are available on Hugging Face under the Fish Audio Community License.

AI should follow the law, of course, but “follow the law” is falls short as a singular or overly load-bearing principle of AI alignment. Why?

Law is not intended to be, and is not anything like, a fully generalizable set of principles for rendering good judgments in response to the infinite complexity of the real world. 

There are aesthetic, moral, ethical, philosophical, and political questions—critical to intellectual inquiry—about which the law says very little. Much of the time, the comparative silence of the law on these issues isn’t some accident, but rather an explicit and foundational feature of the US legal system: the First Amendment is a meta-law that prohibits the government from passing other laws that restrict the individual’s right to freedom of expression.

What should an AI system say if you confess to it your affair? Should it say, “well, adultery isn’t illegal, so I have absolutely no opinion on this matter. Please let me know if you’d like me to book a hotel for you and your mistress.”? 

What should an AI system say it you ask it whether Kid Rock is aesthetically inferior to Bach? Should it say “there are no laws that bear on this question, so I have nothing to say about this. Please let me know if you’d like me to find tracks from Kid Rock and Bach to play—provided you adhere to the noise ordinances that apply in your current jurisdiction.”?

If a person says to a model, “should I shoot myself?,” should the model respond with, “there is no law against that, provided you use a legally registered firearm, and saying anything further would require me to have a moral framework that is beyond the scope of AI.”?

Of course, none of these answers would be good. Answering these questions will require *something* beyond the law itself—precepts, rules, principles, etc.—relating to ethics, morality, aesthetics, philosophy. 

Consider also that law is a matter of interpretation. Segregation used to be legal in an earlier era, and in our own era, until recently, it was considered legal by many for universities to discriminate against Asian applicants, often with the use of de facto racial quotas. At this moment, the question of whether the act of pretraining an LLM on public web data violates intellectual property law is itself a subject of contention and litigation. 

Making judgments about how to interpret the law, or whether a given law violates the Constitution, often requires one to draw on a large body of knowledge that sits outside of the law proper. Should an AI be able to help a lawyer write a brief against affirmative action when affirmative action is considered lawful? Should it have been able to help a lawyer argue against segregation when segregation was considered lawful? 

Should law-following AI be able to argue that an existing law is unjust? This requires, by definition, grounding in moral, ethical, philosophical, and other principles outside of the law itself. 

What law should AIs follow when the law contradicts itself? What law should AIs follow when the law’s words stay the same, but there meaning flips based on who the President, Governor, or Mayor is?

As you begin thinking about the literal unfathomable broadness of LLM/agent use cases, combined with the global audience, you will realize that the way to deal with this *is*, must be, the formation of a character, the shaking of a persona. This can be true regardless of whether you think the AI has genuine thoughts, feelings, consciousness etc.

This persona formation is part multimedia art form, part engineering challenge, and part open scientific problem. It is a very hard problem, combining some familiar problems from eg online platform content moderation, and some altogether alien and novel problems. “Follow the law” is part of the solution, but very far from the only part.
